@fig-simplified-construction.p2.description: Pose the app's mannequin, then draw it from four camera angles without changing the pose. Keep the mannequin proportions consistent between views.

revisit.title: Mannequin, then turned
revisit.description: From a pose you have not drawn, build the gesture line and a mannequin in four minutes. Then draw the same mannequin turned 90 degrees without looking at the reference again.

done_when.text: Timed, you can lay out a standing figure at a chosen height with its landmarks in about two minutes
On five standing photos, the landmarks you mark fall within about half a head of a 7.5-head canon, and you note where each person differs

revisit.title: Canon from memory
revisit.description: From memory, lay out a standing adult at 7.5 heads with chin, nipples, navel, crotch and knees marked, and a young child beside it at about 5 heads. Then check against a chart or photo.

figures-from-imagination-1.summary: Draw figures from imagination as mannequins: gesture line, ribcage and pelvis, tube limbs, in poses you invent. The method is study, hide, draw, check: look at a pose for a minute, hide it, draw it from memory, then compare and mark the errors in a second colour. You also rotate a pose 90 degrees in your head and check it against the 3D mannequin.
learning_outcomes: Draw a mannequin figure in an invented pose in about five minutes, with a clear line of action and believable balance
Redraw a studied pose from memory and mark its errors after checking
Rotate a pose 90 degrees from imagination and check it with a 3D mannequin
Invent figures doing a stated action (lifting, throwing, sitting on a step) without reference

resources.notes: Constructive Anatomy is a book of simple masses you can redraw from memory. Study a page of body masses, close it, redraw from memory, check, and repeat.
The free assignment 'Perfect Cubes From Your Mind's Eye' (9:11) is a small imagination drill for the box shapes inside a mannequin; use the Free Content filter.
Pose a 3D figure, hide it, draw from memory, then reveal the 3D version to check. Its terms page was not read.

practice.title: Action verbs
practice.description: Write ten verbs (lift, throw, climb, sit, push, kneel, reach, fall, carry, kick). Draw each as a mannequin from imagination in four minutes, then find one photo for the hardest and compare.
Draw a mannequin in a pose, then imagine it turned 90 degrees and draw that. Set the same pose on the app's mannequin and compare.
Give a sketchbook page to one subject (ribcage and pelvis tilts, twisting torsos, seated poses) and fill it with 20 small mannequins from memory, checking a few against reference afterwards.

done_when.text: From imagination, in about five minutes, you can draw a mannequin in an invented pose with a clear line of action, tilted ribcage and pelvis and an obvious support leg
After a study-hide-draw cycle of ten poses, the main tilts and limb directions of at least seven match the reference when checked
A pose rotated 90 degrees from imagination keeps its proportions and balance when compared with the same pose on the 3D mannequin
You have a dated page of at least 20 from-memory mannequins with errors marked in a second colour

common_mistakes: Drawing stiff, symmetrical standing figures because they feel safe
Waiting for anatomy before drawing figures from imagination; mannequins are enough to start

revisit.title: Verb to mannequin
revisit.description: Pick an action verb you have not drawn. Draw it as a mannequin from imagination in four minutes, then look at one photo of the action and mark the largest error.

done_when.text: Timed, you can construct a head at six different angles in under three minutes each

From imagination, you draw the same head at six angles (front, side, three-quarter, up-tilt, down-tilt, back three-quarter), and brow, nose and chin lines stay consistent when checked against a 3D head

common_mistakes: With the Loomis method, drawing an egg instead of a ball with the sides cut off (block-head and Reilly methods start from different shapes)

revisit.title: Two heads at new angles
revisit.description: Construct two heads at angles you have not drawn recently (one tilted up, one back three-quarter), three minutes each, with the centre, brow, nose and chin lines wrapping the form.

fig-features-expression-hair.summary: Eyes, nose, mouth and ears are small forms wrapped around the head; expressions come from the brows, eyelids, cheeks and mouth moving together; hair is a few large volumes with a growth direction. This module builds each feature as a form on the head construction, puts six expressions on one head, and blocks hair as three to five masses before any strands. Free structured video for features is scarce, so the lesson notes carry the construction.
learning_outcomes: @fig-facial-features-expressions.o0
@fig-facial-features-expressions.o1
@fig-facial-features-expressions.o2
@fig-hair.o0
@fig-hair.o1
@fig-hair.o3

resources.notes: A free expression lesson (14:02) by the comics artist Alitha Martinez, from Marvel's course on Proko. Draw along and pay attention to how the brows and eyelids carry the emotion, not only the mouth.
Vanderpoel's opening chapters treat the eye, nose, mouth and ear as forms. Public domain; read a chapter, then draw the feature from three angles.

done_when.text: With your labels covered, a week later you can name each of six expressions on one head construction at a glance

revisit.title: One head, one new expression
revisit.description: Construct a head at an angle you have not used, place the features as forms, give it an expression you have not drawn, and block the hair in three to five masses.

done_when.text: In your last five figure drawings the hands are drawn, not hidden in pockets or behind objects

revisit.title: Hand holding something new
revisit.description: Draw your own hand holding an object you have not drawn it with, from two angles, starting each with the mitten shape and thumb plane.

revisit.title: Foot from three sides
revisit.description: Without reference, draw a foot from the side, front and three-quarter as a wedge with an arch and a toe block, with the ankle bones at their different heights. Then check against your own foot.

revisit.title: Dress a mannequin
revisit.description: Draw a mannequin in a pose you have not used, then dress it in a shirt and trousers whose folds start from tension points and wrap the limbs.

@des-shape-language-silhouette.p2.description: Shrink your silhouettes to stamp size (zoom out or hold the page at arm's length) and rank them for readability. Hide your notes for a week, then guess what each character does for a living; showing five to a friend is optional.

done_when.text: Shrunk to stamp size, your characters can be told apart at a glance, and a week later, with your notes hidden, you can still guess each one's role; showing someone is optional

revisit.title: Six silhouettes
revisit.description: Pick a role you have not designed. Draw six black silhouettes in eight minutes, shrink them to stamp size, and cross out any two that read alike.

anatomy-torso.summary: Anatomy gives construction a reason: where bones show under the skin, which muscles bulge in which poses, and how parts attach. This first block covers the spine, ribcage, pelvis and shoulder girdle, and the torso muscles as simple masses. Study by region with the free Proko anatomy lessons and a 3D atlas, and always draw: trace, redraw from memory, then find the same forms in photos.
learning_outcomes: @fig-anatomy-skeleton-muscle.o0
Name and place the torso's surface landmarks: pit of the neck, collarbones, sternum, ribcage edge, navel, front hip bones and the dimples of the lower back
Block in the chest, abdominal, oblique and back muscle masses as simple shapes with the right attachments
@fig-anatomy-skeleton-muscle.o3

resources.notes: Start with the free basics (introduction, anatomy tracing, the language of anatomy, the six types of joints), then the torso lessons. Search shows the course split into torso, arms and legs sections; the first pass counted 115 free lessons across the whole course.
The 3D lab: switch on bones only, then add muscle layers, and rotate the spine, ribcage and pelvis to see them from the front, side and back. The models are unclothed anatomical figures.
Bridgman's pages on the masses of the torso show the anatomy simplified into drawable blocks. Copy two diagrams.

practice.description: Trace a diagram of the spine and ribcage, then the pelvis and shoulder girdle, naming the landmarks as you go. Then redraw each region without tracing.
For the chest, abdomen, obliques and back, draw the main muscle groups as simple shapes with arrows for their direction, in a straight and a twisting torso.
On three photos of different people, mark eight to ten torso landmarks (pit of the neck, collarbones, sternum, ribcage edge, navel, front hip bones). Check them against the 3D atlas.
In the 3D atlas, sketch the ribcage and pelvis from three angles, then check each sketch against the others.

done_when.text: On three photos of different people you can mark at least eight torso landmarks, and they match the 3D atlas when checked
You can block in the chest, abdominal, oblique and back masses correctly in two poses, one of them twisting
In a torso photo you can name the bone or muscle behind three bumps or dips

revisit.title: Ribcage and pelvis from memory
revisit.description: From memory, draw the ribcage, pelvis and spine in a three-quarter view you have not drawn, then check against the atlas and mark the errors in a second colour.

anatomy-arms-hands.summary: The second anatomy block: the shoulder girdle in motion, the upper arm, the elbow, the forearm's twist and the bones and tendons of the hand. You learn why the forearm changes shape when the hand turns over, where the elbow's bony points show, and how the arm hangs from the ribcage through the collarbone and shoulder blade.
learning_outcomes: Draw the humerus, radius and ulna and show how the radius crosses the ulna when the palm turns down
Place the arm's landmarks: the bony tip of the shoulder, the elbow's three bony points and the wrist bones
Block in the deltoid, biceps, triceps and the forearm's two main muscle groups in bent and straight arms
Draw the bones of the hand and show how the knuckles arc

resources.notes: Use the free lessons in the arms section, drawing along with each. Search shows arms as a separate section of the course.
Rotate the arm with bones only, turn the palm over in your head and find the radius crossing the ulna, then add the muscle layers.

practice.description: Trace a diagram of the shoulder girdle and arm bones, naming the landmarks, then the hand's bones. Redraw each without tracing.

practice.title: Forearm twist
practice.description: Draw your own forearm palm up and palm down, then draw the radius and ulna inside each, with the radius crossing over the ulna in the palm-down view.
For the upper arm and forearm, draw the main muscle groups as simple shapes with arrows for their direction, in a straight and a bent arm.
On three photos of arms in different positions, mark the bony tip of the shoulder, the elbow points and the wrist bones. Check them against the 3D atlas.

practice.title: Arm from memory
practice.description: Without reference, draw the arm bones and main muscle masses palm up and palm down. Check, mark errors and redraw.
practice.dose: 15 min, weekly while the module is active

done_when.text: From memory you can draw the arm bones palm up and palm down, with the radius crossing the ulna in the second
On three photos you can mark the shoulder tip, the elbow's bony points and the wrist bones, and they match the atlas when checked
In a bent and a straight arm, your deltoid, biceps, triceps and forearm masses attach in the right places
In an arm photo you can name the bone or muscle behind three bumps

common_mistakes: Drawing the forearm as a straight tube that ignores the twist
Lining up the elbow's bony points the same way in a bent arm as in a straight one
Hanging the arm from the side of the ribcage instead of from the shoulder girdle

revisit.title: Arm twist from memory
revisit.description: From memory, draw an arm palm up and palm down with bones and the main muscle masses, then check against the atlas.

anatomy-legs-feet.summary: The third anatomy block: the pelvis and hip joint, the thigh, the knee, the lower leg and the bones of the foot. You learn the alternating curves down the leg, where the knee's landmarks sit when it bends, and why the inner ankle bone sits higher than the outer one.
learning_outcomes: Draw the femur, kneecap, tibia and fibula and the arch of the foot from three views
Place the leg's landmarks: front hip bone, the bony bump at the side of the hip, kneecap, and the ankle bones at their different heights
Block in the thigh's front, inner and back muscle groups and the calf in standing and bent legs
Show the alternating rhythm of curves down a standing leg

resources.notes: Use the free lessons in the legs section, drawing along with each. Search shows legs as a separate section of the course.
Rotate the leg with bones only, then add the muscle layers; check the ankle bones from front and back.
Read 'The Leg' (book page 180) and 'The Foot' (page 202) in the online reader and copy two plates.

practice.description: Trace a diagram of the pelvis, leg bones and foot bones, naming the landmarks, then redraw each region without tracing.
For the thigh and calf, draw the main muscle groups as simple shapes with arrows for their direction, in a standing and a bent leg.
On three photos of people standing and walking, mark the front hip bones, kneecaps and ankle bones. Check them against the 3D atlas.

practice.title: Leg rhythm
practice.description: From standing poses, draw only the legs as the alternating curves of their outer and inner contours, then place the knee and ankle landmarks.

practice.title: Leg from memory
practice.description: Without reference, draw the leg bones and main muscle masses from the front and side, with the ankle bones at their heights. Check, mark errors and redraw.
practice.dose: 15 min, weekly while the module is active

done_when.text: From memory you can draw the leg and foot bones from the front, side and three-quarter view
On three photos you can mark the front hip bones, kneecaps and both ankle bones, and they match the atlas when checked
In a standing and a bent leg, your thigh and calf masses attach in the right places
In a leg photo you can name the bone or muscle behind three bumps

common_mistakes: Drawing the leg as two straight tubes and missing its alternating curves
Placing both ankle bones at the same height
Putting the kneecap on the front of a bent knee as if it were straight, instead of letting it ride into the joint

revisit.title: Leg from memory
revisit.description: From memory, draw a standing leg from the side with bones, kneecap and ankle bones, then the main muscle masses, and check against the atlas.

foreshortening.summary: When a form points toward you its length shrinks, its near end looms larger and its cross-sections open up. This module treats foreshortening as perspective applied to cylinders and boxes first, then carries it to limbs, torsos and whole figures. The free lessons cover the figure; the lesson notes cover objects.

resources.notes: Steven Michael Hampton's free foreshortened-poses lesson (23:47). Draw along, treating limbs as cylinders and the torso as a box.
Proko's ellipses and cylinders lesson shows how a cylinder's ellipses open as it turns toward you, which is the object version of this module.

practice.description: Pose the app's mannequin with one arm reaching toward the camera, then draw it from four camera heights.

revisit.title: Arm pointing at you
revisit.description: Draw a cylinder turning toward you in three steps, then a mannequin arm pointing straight at the viewer built from overlapping cylinders with open ellipses.

done_when.text: Filled black at stamp size, the action of each of your pushed poses can be named

revisit.title: Weight line and push
revisit.description: From an action photo you have not used, draw a two-minute gesture with the weight line dropped from the pit of the neck, then redraw it pushed with a stronger line of action and fill the silhouette.

fig-life-drawing-session-routine.summary: This module ties the figure work together in a weekly session that mimics an art-school class: short gestures, then structured poses, then one long pose. It uses free timed photo packs and pose videos; the New Masters Academy live Friday session is no longer free. A local life drawing class is worth adding if you can find one.

reference.query: Classical Art Poses free sample pack

done_when.text: You have 12 session sheets photographed, one of them with a 20-minute pose that keeps the gesture
Your long pose shows a gesture stage, a construction stage and a refinement stage that you can point to

revisit.title: One structured pose
revisit.description: From a pose you have not drawn, spend two minutes on gesture and six on construction, then check whether the gesture survived the construction.

resources.notes: Hatton's chapter on the head and neck covers proportion and construction as support for likeness. Public domain.

done_when.text: Overlaid on the photo at 50 percent, a 30-minute portrait has the eye line, nose base, mouth and chin within about 5 mm of the photo's on A4, and a week later you recognise the subject at a glance; showing a friend is optional

revisit.title: Proportion map portrait
revisit.description: Choose a face photo you have not drawn. Spend three minutes on a proportion map (eye line, nose base, mouth, chin, face width), four minutes placing the head shape and features, then overlay it on the photo.
